column3: Exact parallel: a community declares that it will not be punished.
God's expansion and restriction of provision directly overturn wealth as proof of security.
It answers wrongdoers with enduring punishment according to what they earned.
It repeats the exemption-from-punishment formula, though here it is voiced by the saved.
The same surah counters denial of the Hour with its certain arrival and complete divine knowledge.
It assigns evil punishment and ultimate loss to those who deny the Hereafter.
A closely related denial joins worldly-life reduction with rejection of resurrection.
Immediate reply: provision is expanded or restricted by the Lord, not evidence of immunity.

Earlier peoples had greater wealth and children yet ended as losers.

Love of wealth and sons is presented as worldly attraction, not enduring standing.
It repeats that wealth and children will not avail disbelievers against God.
A disbeliever's respite is not good for them but an increase in sin before punishment.
An abundance of evil must not impress, qualifying material plenty as a value claim.
Opened worldly abundance precedes sudden seizure, decisively separating prosperity from safety.
The people of the Heights tell the arrogant that their amassed wealth and pride did not avail them.
Wealth and children are explicitly identified as a trial rather than proof of favor.
Pharaoh and his chiefs receive worldly adornment and wealth that becomes part of their misguidance and judgment.
Those seeking only worldly life and its adornment receive it here but have no share in the Hereafter.
It completes the warning: their works fail and the Fire is their final portion.
A secure and well-provided town is made to taste hunger and fear after disbelief.
When a town is to be destroyed, its affluent leaders transgress and the decree is fulfilled against it.
Worldly gifts are extended to both groups and are not withheld from God's bounty.
God expands and restricts provision with knowledge, directly correcting status claims drawn from wealth.
It opens the two-garden comparison that exposes false confidence in abundant property.
The garden owner enters his wealth wronging himself, supplying the focal boast's moral diagnosis.
He expects his garden never to perish and anticipates an even better return, paralleling presumed immunity.
His companion rebukes his disbelief and directs him back to the Creator rather than property.
The boastful owner's property is destroyed, overturning confidence in its permanence.
His wealth leaves him without a supporting faction or power to recover it.
Wealth and children are only worldly adornment, while enduring righteous deeds are better with God.
God will record the claimant's words and extend punishment to him.
God inherits the claimed wealth and children, and the claimant returns alone.

It answers that the affluent recipients do not perceive the real meaning of that extension.
When affluent people are seized by punishment, their former status does not preserve them.
On the Day of Judgment neither wealth nor children will benefit anyone.
Qarun's immense riches establish the prosperity narrative that follows.
Qarun attributes his wealth to personal knowledge, paralleling self-grounded material confidence.
Observers desire Qarun's worldly portion, illustrating the attraction of visible abundance.
Qarun and his house are swallowed by the earth despite their wealth.
It asks whether people see that God expands and restricts provision, making it a sign rather than rank.
The arrogant and the oppressed dispute responsibility for rejecting guidance, extending the focal social setting.
The oppressed expose the leaders' plotting and their concealment of disbelief, clarifying the elite's influence.

The consequences of their evil deeds overtake earlier claimants despite their prior worldly position.

God distributes worldly livelihood among people, denying that it establishes inherent superiority.
Even the disbelievers could receive lavish worldly goods without that signaling approval.
The listed material luxuries show that earthly abundance can be granted without signaling approval.
All such worldly adornment is temporary enjoyment; the Hereafter belongs to the God-conscious.
Those who exhausted their good things in worldly life are met with humiliating punishment.
Neither wealth nor children will avail their possessors against God at all.

Wealth and children are explicitly a trial, while the greater reward is with God.
The garden owners' trial begins a narrative of abundance being removed through wrongful intent.
A condemned speaker confesses that his wealth did not avail him.
A resistant man is described as having been granted abundant wealth.
His sons are also made present to him, matching the focal markers of worldly status.
Despite those gifts, he greedily expects further increase rather than receiving immunity.
The wealthy resister is assigned a severe ascent in punishment.
A person wrongly reads ease and bounty as proof that his Lord has honored him.

His belief that no one sees him is a secondary analogue to unaccountable self-confidence.
Wealth will not avail a person when he falls into ruin.

It gives self-sufficiency as the explicit cause of that transgression.

Abu Lahab's wealth and earnings do not avail him against judgment.
